tagline: Covered bridges trace an engineer’s work across the Darby country
intro: The Big Darby Plains Scenic Byway’s main route parallels Big Darby Creek for more than 27 miles. Ohio’s Department of Transportation includes the road in its byways collection, highlighting covered bridges, nature preserves, century farms, cemeteries and historic homes. The creek itself carries both state and national scenic designations.

The corridor’s bridge-building history centers on Reuben Partridge, who developed a new truss and brace system after seeing local bridges fail under the stress of heavy rain. He patented his U-shaped truss in 1872 and built more than 200 bridges across Union County and central Ohio during his lifetime. His Bigelow Bridge was later strengthened with internal steel supports; his Reed Bridge collapsed in 1993.

Traveling from Milford Center toward Unionville Center brings you through Bridgeport, where Buck Run meets Big Darby Creek. A separate excursion to Axe Handle Road reaches Bigelow Bridge over Little Darby Creek, between Irwin and Chuckery. Farther southeast, Plain City stands along Big Darby Creek.

moments.title: Bigelow Bridge
moments.text: Bigelow Bridge carries a wooden bridge-builder’s work reinforced with steel. Reuben Partridge built the crossing in 1873, the year after he patented his U-shaped truss design. Partridge developed his truss and brace system to handle stresses from heavy rain and vehicle traffic. Named for nearby resident Eliphas Bigelow, it crosses Little Darby Creek on Axe Handle Road between Irwin and Chuckery. A 1990 refurbishment added internal steel supports, and the bridge was repainted in 2008. In 2010, the Ohio Historical Society dedicated a marker honoring both the bridge and the surrounding Darby Plains.

moments.title: Reed Bridge
moments.text: Reed Bridge is a crossing to understand through its absence. Reuben Partridge built this single-span wooden covered bridge over Big Darby Creek in 1884. At more than 150 feet, it was Union County’s longest covered bridge. Route 38 bypassed it in the 1960s; National Register listing followed in 1975. The bridge collapsed on August 19, 1993.

moments.title: Unionville Center
moments.text: Unionville Center marks its connection to Charles W. Fairbanks with a festival held each May. The future U.S. senator and vice president was born and raised here. The village began as Unionville, laid out in 1847; its post office followed in 1848 and incorporation in 1879.
